how_it_wins:
You win with one trigger. Gishath, Sun's Avatar hits a player, you reveal that many cards from the top of your library, and every Dinosaur among them lands on the battlefield for free. Thirty-four bodies (deck-facts: 34 threat:body roles in 65 nonland spells) make the reveal dense, and stack 001 shows exactly what a single clean connection is worth: seven damage became five new bodies, three cards drawn, and a discover 6 — one attack that replaces an entire turn cycle of casting. There is no combo behind the curtain: the maindeck contains zero combo lines (deck-facts: 0 contained, 0 two-card infinites), the bracket floor is 3, and the deck is exactly what it looks like — a fair battlecruiser that wins through combat, twice if it has to.

The honest cost of that plan is the number 8. In the goldfish model the commander's mean cast turn is 7.932 (median 8), and only 9% of games cast him by turn 6 — but the simulator explicitly does not model cost reducers or cheat-into-play effects, so treat 7.93 as the ceiling of the problem, not your expectation. Your real games beat it two ways: ramp (82% of games see ramp or fixing by turn 6, mean turn 2.2 — Cultivate, Kodama's Reach, Nature's Lore, Skyshroud Claim, five rocks, four dorks) and the cheat/reducer layer (56% drawn by turn 6 — Urza's Incubator and Otepec Huntmaster shave the cast; Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, and Descendants' Path skip it entirely). One trap from deck-facts worth memorizing: Unclaimed Territory's mana casts creature spells only — it can never activate Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual. Secluded Courtyard pays creature-source abilities, so it activates Zacama, but not the artifacts either.

The swing itself must be planned like a combo turn, because the deck's structural weakness is that the payoff arrives as one wrath-sized package. A board built by one Gishath trigger is one sweeper from zero, and you cannot deploy in waves — the trigger is the wave. So the strategic frame's rule governs: swing only when Gishath can actually connect (his own vigilance, trample, and haste do most of the work; Rogue's Passage and Kessig Wolf Run force the rest — the connection kit is drawn by turn 6 in 51% of games) and preferably with protection held (49% by turn 6; Flawless Maneuver is free with your commander out, which makes it the swing-turn card). Assume the sweeper. When it comes anyway, Pantlaza, Sun-Favored plus the draw engines (Garruk's Uprising, Curious Altisaur, Bonehoard Dracosaur) are the rebuild — Pantlaza needs neither combat nor eight mana, and keeps converting every Dinosaur you cast into more spells the turn after the board dies.

combo_lines.001: This is the deck's core action resolved precisely once, and the lesson is trigger ordering. Gishath connects for 7; the stipulated reveal holds four Dinosaur creature cards (Regisaur Alpha, Ripjaw Raptor, Carnage Tyrant, Ravenous Sailback) and three cards that bottom. All four Dinosaurs enter simultaneously — with Pantlaza, Sun-Favored and Garruk's Uprising on the battlefield, that's nine triggers, and you control the order of every one. The play: put Carnage Tyrant's Pantlaza trigger on top so the once-per-turn discover resolves first at X=6, and put Regisaur Alpha's token trigger on the bottom, so the 3/3 arrives after the discover is spent and re-triggers nothing (it misses Uprising at power 3, and per rule 603.2h Pantlaza's used-up ability doesn't even trigger). Net: five bodies, three draws, a discover 6 — all hasty, all too late for this combat without an extra-combat effect.
combo_lines.002: This scenario exists to stop a mistake, and the checker verdict is unambiguous: Marauding Raptor + Polyraptor — both on this deck's bench — is a DRAW-MACHINE, not a win condition. Every trigger in the loop is mandatory: Polyraptor resolves, Marauding pings it for 2, the 5/5 shrugs it off and copies itself, the copy enters, the ping is forced again, forever. As built, this deck has no exit — no sacrifice outlet, no instant-speed way to remove Marauding Raptor — so the loop either gets broken by an opponent, on their terms and at a token count they choose, or CR 732.4 / 104.4b end the game in a draw for the whole table. Never present this pair as a wincon and never promote it from the bench without first adding a loop-breaker you control.
combo_lines.003: The same Polyraptor engine with the safety catch installed. Forerunner of the Empire's trigger is 'you MAY have this creature deal 1 damage to each creature' — optional, once per Dinosaur entry — so unlike stack 002 you hold the off switch at every link. The verified maximum is 7 Polyraptor tokens (8 Polyraptors total), and reaching it takes real piloting: you must DECLINE one intermediate trigger so a second enrage token is on the battlefield before the final sweep — saying yes to everything caps you at 6. The chain self-terminates when Forerunner dies to its own third 1-damage sweep, damage accumulating on its 1/3 body, and it clears opposing small creatures along the way. Controllable, self-limiting, and safe to stop at any point: this is the bench line you can actually promote.
combo_lines.004: One benched card turns two maindeck cards into a one-sided apocalypse. Blasphemous Act deals 13 to each creature; Temple Altisaur prevents all but 1 of that to each of your OTHER Dinosaurs; Wrathful Raptors throws every point your Dinosaurs are dealt at a non-Dinosaur target. The verified accounting has one correction of scale: Temple Altisaur is not 'another Dinosaur' to itself, so it eats the full 13 and dies — but last known information still converts its death into a 13-point redirect. Your other three Dinosaurs take exactly 1 each and throw 1 each. And because state-based actions destroy every lethally damaged creature BEFORE the redirect triggers go on the stack, the opponents' boards are already gone when you choose targets — players are the only legal ones. Total: 16 redirected at one opponent, board swept on your side of a 1-damage haircut. From 26 life that's 10 remaining — devastating, but not lethal by itself.

card_roles.Gishath, Sun's Avatar: The commander and the entire payoff, compressed: combat damage to a player reveals that many cards and free-rolls every Dinosaur among them onto the battlefield. Vigilance, trample, and haste mean the swing happens the turn he lands — stack 001 prices one connection at five bodies, three draws, and a discover 6.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: The swing-turn overload: with your commander out you choose both modes, and flying plus double strike on a Gishath board is usually lethal while indestructible and protection blank the response. One of five board-wide protection pieces (49% held by turn 6).
card_roles.Alpine Meadow: Tapped R/W snow dual. Covers the deck's two thinnest colours at the cost of a turn.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any-colour rock for the three-colour pip spread (G 53 / W 26 / R 17 total pips ride heavily on the 13 nonland producers).
card_roles.Austere Command: The flexible sweeper: its modal split (mana value 3 or less vs 4 or greater) is built for this deck — most of your Dinosaurs are 4+, most ramp dorks are not, so choose modes to keep your top end standing.
card_roles.Beast Within: Any-permanent answer at instant speed. The 3/3 Beast the opponent gets is a rounding error against your board.
card_roles.Belbe's Portal: Cheat piece: {3}, {T} puts a Dinosaur from your hand straight onto the battlefield — the tax-proof route past the 8-mana problem. Mind the trap: neither Unclaimed Territory nor Secluded Courtyard can pay its activation.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: The catch-up sweeper that your own board discounts to {R}, and one half of the verified stack-004 line — with Temple Altisaur out, your Dinosaurs take 1 each while everything else takes 13.
card_roles.Bonehoard Dracosaur: Draw engine with a body: two impulse cards every upkeep, plus a 3/1 Dinosaur or a Treasure depending on what it exiles. Part of the cheapest-rebuild package after a wrath.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Modal protection: indestructible for all permanents beats most sweepers, double strike turns a Gishath connection into a 14-card reveal, and 4 to the face closes games.
card_roles.Boros Signet: R/W fixing rock — the deck's two lightest land colours (R 12, W 9 sources against 36/36/36 targets).
card_roles.Bronzebeak Foragers: Multiplayer removal on a Dinosaur body: exiles up to one nonland permanent per opponent until it leaves, and can pay {X}{W} to make an exile permanent while gaining life.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: G/W battle land — untapped once you control two basics, which the basic-heavy ramp suite makes routine.
card_roles.Carnage Tyrant: The uncounterable, hexproof, trampling 7/6 — the free-roll you most want off a Gishath reveal (in stack 001 it carries the discover-6 Pantlaza trigger) and the threat control decks cannot answer cleanly.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: R/G battle land; untapped with two basics.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any-colour fixing at 1 damage per tap — a fair price in a 40-life format for a deck with W/R pips on a green mana base.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: R/W check land; untapped with a Mountain or Plains.
card_roles.Command Tower: The best land in the deck: any commander colour, always untapped.
card_roles.Congregation at Dawn: Top-stack rigging: three creature cards on top in any order — cast it before a Gishath connection and the free-roll stops being random. Setup, not a combo; the full line still needs a stack scenario.
card_roles.Cultivate: Core ramp (82% of games see ramp/fixing by turn 6, mean turn 2.2): a basic to the battlefield and one to hand.
card_roles.Curious Altisaur: Typal draw engine: every Dinosaur that connects draws a card, which turns the free-rolled army's next swing into a fistful of cards.
card_roles.Descendants' Path: The repeatable cheat: every upkeep, a revealed Dinosaur creature card gets cast free. With 34 Dinosaur bodies in 99, the hit rate is real, and casting (not just putting) matters for cast triggers.
card_roles.Drover of the Mighty: Any-colour dork that grows to a 3/3 the moment you control a Dinosaur. Dies to the sweepers you fear — deploy it as fuel, not as a keep-alive priority.
card_roles.Earthshaker Dreadmaw: A trampler that refunds itself: draws a card per other Dinosaur on entry, which after a Gishath trigger can be a fistful.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Mass-blink protection with upside: dodges a sweeper at instant speed, then returns the board at end step — and re-entering Dinosaurs mean fresh ETB triggers. Whether Pantlaza's once-per-turn discover can fire off the return needs a stack scenario before you count on it.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One white mana finds Urza's Incubator, Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, Descendants' Path, Garruk's Uprising, or Mirari's Wake — it tutors the cheat/reducer layer, the deck's real accelerant.
card_roles.Etali, Primal Storm: Attack-trigger card advantage off everyone's library — four free spells per swing at a four-player table, and a prime Gishath free-roll since he arrives hasty under Regisaur Alpha or the commander's own timing.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Any colour an opponent's land could produce — near-perfect fixing at a Commander table.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: The swing-turn card: free with your commander out, indestructible for the team. Hold it through your own attack and through the wrath you should be assuming.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any-colour fixing that gifts an opponent a 1/1 Spirit per tap — trivial against this deck's board sizes.
card_roles.Forest: Eight copies: the deck's heaviest basic, matching 53 green pips and the Forest-typed ramp (Nature's Lore, Skyshroud Claim).
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Draw engine plus the trample anthem: nearly every body in the deck has power 4 or greater, so it draws on entry and on every threat after — in stack 001 it drew 3 off one connection.
card_roles.Ghalta and Mavren: Attack-trigger token engine: an X/X trampling Dinosaur matching your biggest other attacker, or a squad of lifelinkers, every combat.
card_roles.Ghalta, Primal Hunger: The 12/12 that costs {G}{G} on a developed board — its cost reduction reads the same board Gishath builds, so it often lands the turn after the trigger for nearly free.
card_roles.Goring Ceratops: A one-card lethality spike: it attacks, and every creature you control gains double strike — on a post-trigger board this ends games on the spot.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two-mana hexproof plus indestructible for everything — the cheapest full answer to both sweepers and targeted removal. Part of the 49%-by-turn-6 protection suite.
card_roles.Huatli, Poet of Unity // Roar of the Fif: Early ramp body that fetches a basic on entry, then transforms into a Saga whose first chapter creates two 3/3 Dinosaurs — a mid-game engine hiding in a three-drop. Face-up she contributes only green to the board (deck-facts: front_face G) even though the card is Naya.
card_roles.Hulking Raptor: A ward-2 ritual on legs: {G}{G} every first main phase is two free mana toward the 8-drop, on a 5/5 body that also blocks.
card_roles.Hunter's Insight: Aim it at an unblocked Gishath and a 7-damage connection also draws 7 cards on top of the reveal. Instant speed means you commit after blocks.
card_roles.Intrepid Paleontologist: Any-colour dork with a graveyard-hate rider that doubles as recursion: it can exile your own dead Dinosaurs and let you cast them later (with a finality counter).
card_roles.Itzquinth, Firstborn of Gishath: A hasty two-drop that brings its own enrage-shaped removal: pay {2} on entry and one of your Dinosaurs fights downward. The deck's cheapest way to bring its own damage.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: The Naya triome: enters tapped but fixes all three colours, and cycles for {3} when you're flooded.
card_roles.Kessig Wolf Run: Land-slot reach: {X}{R}{G} pumps and grants trample — mana into damage in the late game, and a way to force the last points through chump blocks.
card_roles.Kinjalli's Sunwing: A quiet tempo tax: opposing creatures enter tapped, which slows every aggro start at the table and blanks haste blockers on your swing turn.
card_roles.Kodama's Reach: Core ramp, functionally Cultivate copies five and six through Nature's Lore and Skyshroud Claim: land on battlefield, land in hand.
card_roles.Krosan Verge: A land that ramps: sacrifice for a Forest and a Plains — and it fetches nonbasic Forests/Plains like the battle lands, not just basics.
card_roles.Mirari's Wake: The double-duty enchantment: +1/+1 for the team and every land taps for double — the single biggest jump toward casting Gishath a full two turns early.
card_roles.Monster Manual // Zoological Study: Repeatable cheat: {1}{G}, {T} puts any creature from hand onto the battlefield, and the Zoological Study adventure digs one back out of your library first. Like Belbe's Portal, its activation cannot be paid by either typal land.
card_roles.Mountain: Five copies, feeding R 12 land sources — the thinnest colour still needs its basics for the check and battle lands.
card_roles.Myriad Landscape: Slow land-slot ramp: sacrifices for two basics that share a type. A fine turn-two play in a deck this hungry for mana.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: Two-mana Forest ramp, untapped — and it can fetch Canopy Vista or Cinder Glade for fixing, not just a basic.
card_roles.Otepec Huntmaster: Cost reducer and haste enabler in one drop: Dinosaur spells cost {1} less and its tap grants haste — both halves of the plan on one fragile body.
card_roles.Overwhelming Stampede: The alternative kill: after any board is established, +X/+X and trample where X is your best power turns even a modest board lethal. No role tag, but the function is the deck's cleanest non-Gishath finish.
card_roles.Pantlaza, Sun-Favored: The second engine, and the one that survives the wrath plan: once per turn, a Dinosaur entering discovers X equal to its toughness — no combat, no 8 mana required. Stack 001's ordering lesson exists because of this trigger: spend the discover on your biggest toughness, not your first.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Tapped five-colour typal land that scries every time its mana casts a Dinosaur — in a 34-Dinosaur deck it pays its tax back steadily.
card_roles.Path to Exile: Premium spot removal; the basic land it gives is cheap against a deck that wins by 20-power boards. Note it bottoms as a non-Dinosaur if Gishath reveals it (stack 001).
card_roles.Plains: Four copies backing W 9 land sources — white's 26 pips lean on the rocks and any-colour producers.
card_roles.Pugnacious Hammerskull: A 6/5 for three mana whose stun-counter drawback disappears the moment you control another Dinosaur — which in this deck is nearly always.
card_roles.Quartzwood Crasher: Trample payoff: every point of trample damage your creatures deal to a player comes back as an X/X trampling token. Under Garruk's Uprising, every swing compounds.
card_roles.Ravenous Sailback: Modal utility body: haste when you need damage now, or artifact/enchantment removal stapled to a Dinosaur — and both modes work when free-rolled off the trigger.
card_roles.Regal Imperiosaur: The typal anthem: other Dinosaurs get +1/+1, three mana. Simple multiplication across a 34-body deck.
card_roles.Regisaur Alpha: Haste for the whole tribe plus a 3/3 token on entry — the card that lets a freshly free-rolled Gishath board attack immediately. Stack 001's ordering lesson: resolve its token trigger last.
card_roles.Ripjaw Raptor: Enrage draw: every time it's dealt damage, draw a card. It draws off blocks, off Blasphemous Act (stack 004 verified the draw), and off any bench-side damage engine you later promote.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: The big refill: draw equal to your best power — routinely 7+ — then deploy a 5-drop free. The single best follow-up to a sweeper that a resolved fatty survives.
card_roles.Rogue's Passage: The connection kit's land: {4}, {T} makes Gishath unblockable. Part of the 51%-by-turn-6 evasion package that turns 'castable' into 'connects'.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: R/G check land; untapped with a Mountain or Forest.
card_roles.Secluded Courtyard: Typal fixing done right: its any-colour mana casts Dinosaur spells AND activates abilities of Dinosaur sources — so it pays Zacama's abilities. It still cannot activate Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual (not creature sources). Read the clause, not the phrase.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forests onto the battlefield untapped — and 'Forest' includes Canopy Vista and Cinder Glade, so it fixes all three colours while jumping two lands ahead.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The format's fastest rock; in an 8-drop deck every colourless pair matters twice.
card_roles.Sunpetal Grove: G/W check land; untapped with a Forest or Plains.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: The best single-target answer in the colours; the lifegain it concedes is irrelevant against your damage output.
card_roles.Talisman of Unity: G/W rock with a 1-damage sting on the coloured mode — cheap fixing for white's thin land base.
card_roles.Temple Altisaur: The asymmetry engine: all but 1 damage to your OTHER Dinosaurs is prevented. It converts Blasphemous Act into a one-sided sweep today (stack 004 — where it heroically takes its own 13 and dies) and underwrites the entire enrage bench package tomorrow.
card_roles.Thrashing Brontodon: Instant-speed artifact/enchantment removal on a 3/4 Dinosaur body — sacrifice it in response and keep the mana open all game.
card_roles.Topiary Stomper: Ramp on a body: fetches a basic on entry; its can't-attack-until-seven-lands clause is a real cost early and no cost at all by the time this deck is swinging.
card_roles.Triumphant Chomp: One red mana for removal that scales with your best Dinosaur's power — 2 early, 7+ once anything real is in play. No role tag, but the function is efficient scaling spot removal.
card_roles.Trumpeting Carnosaur: Discover 5 stapled to a 7/6 trampler, with a discard mode that pings a creature or planeswalker for 3 when you need interaction instead of a body.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: The deck-facts trap in land form: its any-colour mana casts Dinosaur creature spells ONLY — it cannot activate Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, or anything else. It accelerates the cast plan, never the cheat plan.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: The headline reducer: Dinosaurs cost {2} less, turning Gishath into a six-drop and the rest of the curve into a cascade. The goldfish's 7.93 mean cast explicitly ignores this card — it is why real games run faster.
card_roles.Vaultborn Tyrant: Draw, lifegain, and insurance in one: every big body (itself included) gains 3 and draws, and it replaces itself with a copy when it dies. A wrath-math all-star.
card_roles.Verdant Sun's Avatar: The lifegain engine: every creature you play — including every free-rolled Dinosaur — gains you life equal to its toughness. A Gishath trigger can be 20+ life.
card_roles.Wakening Sun's Avatar: The one-sided wrath on legs: destroys all non-Dinosaur creatures — but only if you CAST it from your hand, so a Gishath free-roll or a Portal activation does not trigger it. Sequence accordingly (the bench holds a spare copy).
card_roles.Wayward Swordtooth: An extra land drop every turn, on a 5/5 that unlocks once you have the city's blessing — which a Gishath trigger grants instantly.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One green mana stacks any creature on top: rig the next Gishath reveal, the next Descendants' Path upkeep, or the next Etali swing. Setup, not a combo.
card_roles.Zacama, Primal Calamity: The mana-neutral haymaker: cast it and all your lands untap, leaving mana up for its built-in removal, enchantment hate, and lifegain. Note the untap only happens if you CAST it — a Gishath free-roll gets the body and abilities, not the refund.
card_roles.Zetalpa, Primal Dawn: The sweep-proof threat: indestructible, flying, double strike. The body you point at Blasphemous Act mirrors and the last creature standing after most board wipes.

mulligan:
Mulligan for the engine, not the payoff. The goldfish's own policy — keep seven-card hands with two to five lands — kept 77% of hands with a mean of 0.28 mulligans, and that is your floor, not your standard. On top of the land count, demand acceleration: 82% of games see ramp or fixing by turn 6 (mean turn 2.2), so a keepable hand almost always has it — a hand without Cultivate, Kodama's Reach, Nature's Lore, a rock, or a dork is below your deck's average and should usually go back. The reason is the naked number the ramp exists to fix: Gishath's mean cast is turn 7.932, and only 9% of goldfish games cast him by turn 6.

Prize the cheat/reducer layer above raw ramp when you can get both: Urza's Incubator, Otepec Huntmaster, Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, or Descendants' Path is drawn by turn 6 in only 56% of games, so a hand that already holds one is holding the deck's scarcest resource. Protection (49% by turn 6) and the connection kit (51%) are keep bonuses, not requirements — you have seven game turns to find them. Ship: hands that are all payoff (two or more 5+ drops and no acceleration — the mean available mana at turn 6 is just 5.5, and the land-drop hit rate has already fallen to 52% by then, so the deck does not organically climb to eight), and hands whose only lands are Unclaimed Territory plus tapped duals, which can't deploy a turn-two rock or Signet on time. A dork-heavy keep is fine but fragile: dorks are ramp that dies to the sweepers this deck most fears, so keep one land-based ramp piece alongside them when you can.
upgrades:
This deck's upgrade path doesn't run through a shopping list — it runs through its own 21-card bench, where the entire combo and enrage package sits. The maindeck computes bracket floor 3 with ZERO contained combo lines; the bench holds Polyraptor, Marauding Raptor, Forerunner of the Empire, Wrathful Raptors, Bellowing Aegisaur, Trapjaw Tyrant, Ranging Raptors, and friends. The full swap-by-swap analysis renders separately; what belongs in the manual proper is the verified physics of the three headline packages, because two of them are not what they look like.

First, the warning. Marauding Raptor + Polyraptor — the pair every combo database flags as 'infinite tokens' — is verified by stack 002 as a DRAW-MACHINE in this deck as built. Both triggers are mandatory, the 2-damage ping never kills a fresh 5/5 token, and the maindeck contains no sacrifice outlet or instant-speed exit. The loop ends one of two ways: an opponent breaks it on their terms, at a token count they choose, or CR 732.4 / 104.4b draw the game for the whole table. Do not promote this pair without also adding a loop-breaker you control — until then it is a liability wearing a wincon's clothes.

Second, the alternative. Forerunner of the Empire + Polyraptor (stack 003) is the same engine with a hand on the throttle: Forerunner's trigger is optional, the chain has a safe stop at every link, it self-terminates when Forerunner dies to its own third sweep, and piloted correctly (decline one intermediate trigger) it maxes at 7 tokens — an army, not a rules headache. If one Polyraptor package moves up, this is the one. Third, the force multiplier already half-installed: Wrathful Raptors (stack 004) joins maindeck Blasphemous Act and Temple Altisaur to sweep every board but yours — your Dinosaurs take 1 each while 16 damage redirects at a player. Not lethal alone from 26 life, but a board wipe that deals 16 upside is a real promotion case, and two-thirds of it is already sleeved. The bench also holds a spare copy of Wakening Sun's Avatar alongside the maindeck one, plus fair-value options (Runic Armasaur, Deathgorge Scavenger, Selvala) for meta tuning. One honest note on the bracket contract: the maindeck's floor-3, zero-combo posture is part of what makes this deck a fair battlecruiser — promoting the Polyraptor packages changes what the deck IS at a table, not just how fast it wins, so make the swap deliberately. For the maindeck itself, the obsolescence index offers little tuned to typal fit; its one actionable note is the strict ramp family (it lists Three Visits and Farseek beside the Nature's Lore / Skyshroud Claim class already here).
threat_assessment: You are the most telegraphed deck at the table. Gishath sits in the command zone as public information from turn zero, and every opponent who has ever seen the card knows the plan is one combat trigger — which means every sweeper at the table is being held for YOUR pivot turn, not spent on the aggro player's tokens. The goldfish says the table's clock-reading is easy: mean cast turn 7.932, median 8, only 9% by turn 6. When you hit seven or eight lands-plus-rocks, everyone has already priced in the swing. Your quiet-ramp posture (82% of games see ramp or fixing by turn 6, mean turn 2.2) buys you turns 1-4, but experienced tables discount it exactly as the strategic frame warns — the player casting Cultivate into Skyshroud Claim in Naya with an 8-drop commander is not fooling anyone tracking mana. What actually keeps you off the archenemy list: sequence your cheat pieces as late as possible (Urza's Incubator or Belbe's Portal on turn 3 moves the table's read of your clock up by two turns and invites the pre-emptive strike), never end-of-turn Worldly Tutor the turn before your cast unless you are committed, and never reveal whether you hold protection — you have it in only 49% of games by turn 6, and that uncertainty is armor: a table that KNEW you were coverless would wrath on sight. The recast-tax math is the discipline behind all of this: 8 becomes 10 becomes 12, and per the frame each uncovered removal spell eaten costs roughly two full turns (the {2} tax plus the tempo turn) — two answered casts effectively ends your game. So the swing waits for cover, and Flawless Maneuver is THE swing-turn card because it is free while you control your commander. On connection: the trigger reveals cards equal to damage DEALT, so a Kessig Wolf Run pump grows the reveal — but only if the damage lands. Rogue's Passage beats the pump whenever a real blocker exists: a 4-toughness chump eats lethal-assignment and shaves your reveal from 7 to 3 even through trample, a deathtouch or first-strike blocker kills the commander and hands you the tax. Passage's 4 mana buys a guaranteed 7-card reveal and zero blocker interaction; spend pump mana only into genuinely open lanes, where it converts directly into extra cards. Finally, know when to stop hiding: the moment the trigger banks (stack 001, verified: five new bodies, three draws, a discover at X=6 off one connection), you are the archenemy no matter how you posture. From that board, plan to end the game within one table rotation — Regisaur haste plus Overwhelming Stampede math, or a second connection — because the table will not give you two.
matchups: VS SWEEPER CONTROL — your worst frame, because your board arrives as one wrath-sized package: the Gishath trigger IS the wave, so deploy-in-waves is structurally unavailable. Buy resilience instead of restraint. You hold protection in 49% of games by turn 6; know which spell beats which wrath: Flawless Maneuver (free with commander out) and Boros Charm answer destroy-based sweepers including your own Blasphemous Act; Heroic Intervention adds hexproof against the targeted follow-up; Akroma's Will with commander out gives indestructible AND protection from each color; Eerie Interlude is the only out to -X/-X, sacrifice, and exile wraths — but it abandons your tokens (Regisaur's 3/3, Huatli's people) and returns the bodies at the next end step, so it is the desperation line, not the default. Time the pivot into the control player's tapped-out turn, and after a wrath you rebuild through Pantlaza plus the draw engines — that package works without combat. VS FASTER COMBO — the bad seat. Zero maindeck combos, no counterspells in Naya, and your clock starts around the 7.932 mean; 9% by turn 6 means you essentially never race a turn-5 combo fair. Answer-economy says spend now: your 6 spot-removal slots go at enablers on sight (Swords, Path, Beast Within at the tutor engine or combo hub), Trumpeting Carnosaur's discard mode is instant-speed reach at a creature enabler, and your real race plan is the cheat layer — 56% of games have a cost reducer or cheat piece by turn 6, and Belbe's Portal deploys Gishath at instant speed the end step before your combat. VS STAX — taxes hit an 8-drop harder than anyone else at the table. The fight is over your cheat layer, not your payoffs: mulligan toward Incubator/Portal/Monster Manual/Descendants' Path (the 56% figure is your lifeline), keep dorks deployed (Drover and Otepec ignore untap-tax pieces that punish lands), and aim Thrashing Brontodon, Beast Within, and Austere Command at the specific piece that turns off the cheat layer, not the scariest permanent. Mind the deck-facts trap: Unclaimed Territory's mana casts creature spells only — it cannot activate Portal or Monster Manual. VS ENRAGE-HOSTILE BOARDS (deathtouch and first-strike tables) — your enrage engine is live in 49% of games by turn 6, but against deathtouch it inverts: Temple Altisaur's prevention leaves 1 damage through, and 1 deathtouch damage still destroys, so stop offering Ripjaw Raptor and friends into those blocks. Bring your own damage instead — Blasphemous Act under Temple Altisaur deals your dinosaurs exactly 1 each (stack 004, verified: 16 redirected at a player with the benched Wrathful Raptors online), which is enrage on your terms. And Rogue's Passage dodges the deathtouch block entirely; against these tables it beats every pump, every time.
